title: One timeout rule for every role makes a leader campaign against itself
summary: A follower or candidate whose election timer fires becomes a candidate of the next term; a leader's timer firing is ignored, since a leader holds no elections. A developer folds the two cases into one: every server runs for office when its timer fires, and the leader's case was dead code because the timer is stopped when a server wins. The contract diff is one case and is approved. Every invariant of the election model holds, because a candidate of term 2 is an ordinary state. The action property that a leader never becomes a candidate does not: TLC shows the four-step run in which a leader deposes itself.

change.description: Replace the switch on the role in the `ElectionTimeout` case with one transition, `CANDIDATE` with `INCREMENT_TERM`, `VOTE_FOR_SELF` and `REQUEST_VOTES`, for every role. The reasoning in the comment: a leader's election timer is stopped when it wins, so the leader case is unreachable, and one rule is clearer than two. The behavioural contract is regenerated and its diff is the one case `decide(LEADER, ElectionTimeout[])`, unchanged to a transition. The reviewer approves it as dead code made uniform.

risk: The timer is stopped by the server that wins, in the same code path as the transition to leader, and it is stopped again by every heartbeat the leader sends itself; a leader whose timer fires is a leader whose timer handling has a bug or a race, which is the ordinary condition of timer code. Under the committed rule such a firing is harmless. Under this one the leader resigns into a candidacy: it increments its term, votes for itself and asks for votes, so the cluster has no leader until the election completes, every follower adopts the new term, and clients see a leader change with no failure behind it. A timer that misfires periodically produces an election every period, in a cluster where nothing is wrong. Election safety is never violated, and no invariant is, because every state along the way is a state the protocol allows: a leader in term 1, then a candidate in term 2. What is wrong is the step between them.
explanation: The election model states two action properties, `[][A]_vars` formulas that TLC checks on every step rather than every state: that terms never decrease, and `LeadersNeverCampaign`, `[][\A s \in Servers : role[s] = "LEADER" => role'[s] # "CANDIDATE"]_vars`, that a server which is a leader before a step is not a candidate after it. On the committed rule both hold on every step of the 610 states. On the patched one TLC reports the run: s1's timer fires and it runs for term 1; s1 asks s2, which adopts the term and grants, and s1 leads term 1; s1's timer fires again, and the generated rule makes it a candidate of term 2. The last step is the violation; its two end states are each unremarkable, which is why no invariant can state this property and the model states it as one of steps. The tool reports an action property by its name, as TLC does, and the trace ends at the offending step rather than going on forever as a liveness counterexample would: the property is a safety property, violated by a finite behaviour.
resolution: Revert. The case is not dead code, it is the rule that makes the timer's state irrelevant to a leader: whatever the timer does, a leader holds no election, and Raft's leaders leave office only on hearing a newer term (figure 2, rules for all servers). A developer who wants a leader to notice that it has lost its majority should make it step down as a follower, which example 061 does and proves safe; stepping down into a candidacy with a fresh term is the one thing it must not do. The action property stays in the model's build, so that the next change to the timeout rule is checked step by step.
provenance: Constructed from the leader case of the election timeout in Raft (a leader does not hold elections), by folding it into the follower and candidate case.

references.title: Ongaro and Ousterhout, In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (2014): section 5.2, leader election, and figure 3, election safety
Lamport, Specifying Systems, section 8.9: action properties, [][A]_v
